name: Old money / quiet luxury style

lead: Quiet luxury is understated, high-quality dress with no visible logos, closely related to old money style or stealth wealth. It gives a polished, expensive-looking presentation the moment you wear it.

The look relies on fine materials, tailoring, muted colors and timeless design to suggest taste and wealth quietly. It spread widely in 2023 through the HBO series Succession and media coverage, and was considered dated by early 2024. No studies have tested its effect on attractiveness.

paras: People build outfits from tailored, neutral-toned pieces in good fabrics such as knitwear, trousers, and simple coats, avoiding branding. Fit and fabric quality carry the look, and many buy fewer, better pieces.
No health harms are documented. Commentators note the cost of premium brands and that the look is still a form of status signaling.

Old Money Fashion is Our Favorite Trend in 2023

angle.text: Logo-free, tailored, high-quality clothes make quality and fit show, giving a polished, wealthy-looking presentation straight away. The aesthetic is popular, with no attractiveness studies behind it.

lead: Quiet luxury is a style of dress marked by understated elegance, high-quality materials, timeless design and no visible logos, often used interchangeably with old money style or stealth wealth, though commentators use the terms differently [1][2]. People adopt it to look polished, well-fitted and expensive without branding: tailored neutral pieces, quality fabrics such as cashmere and linen, loafers and simple shoes, and a clean overall silhouette [1][2]. The appearance payoff comes from the whole outfit reading as intentional and put together, and forum members pair it with leanness, a neat haircut and good fit so that the clothes frame the face and physique [3][4].

Old money itself refers to a social class of families that have kept wealth across generations, and the term is used differently in the United States, where it describes a de facto aristocracy, and in the United Kingdom, where it refers more narrowly to nobility and landed gentry [5]. The dress aesthetic borrowed from that world spread twice: first as the TikTok old money aesthetic, with hashtags reported to have passed a billion views by May 2022, and then in 2023 as quiet luxury, carried by the HBO series Succession, post-pandemic spending changes, recession fears and Gwyneth Paltrow's Utah trial wardrobe [1][6]. Commentators considered the trend dated by January 2024, while others argue the underlying look is timeless and still being revived [1][7].

On looksmax.org it is discussed as a way to dress for appeal alongside leanness and grooming, with members debating whether it suits people who are not from that background and whether other aesthetics now have more appeal [3][8][9][4]. Critics and supporters outside the forums argue over whether it is a rejection of logo culture, a form of discreet status signalling, or a style whose associations with privilege make it exclusionary [6][10].

paras: Accounts of the style describe a narrow, repeatable vocabulary. Highsnobiety's menswear guide lists relaxed but clean tailoring, cashmere knitwear, linen shirts, dark and neutral colors, loafers and tennis sneakers, and discreet accessories such as a luxury watch or a cashmere-blend cap, with logos and loud patterns largely absent [2]. A December 2024 campus-newspaper article on the revival adds the cable-knit sweater as a key piece and names Ralph Lauren, J. Crew and Uniqlo as brands that embody the look, with Uniqlo as the more affordable option [7].

TikTok creators covered in a 2022 report on the trend describe handmade loafers, heirloom pearls and cashmere for a mainly American look, and worn-in Barbour jackets and Savile Row suits for a British version, with the idea that clothes are kept until they wear out [6]. Highsnobiety notes that the look can be achieved on modest budgets, so expensive pieces are optional [2]. A forum reply in one thread suggests a Massimo Dutti outfit with shoes for about 200 euros [3].

Wikipedia distinguishes stealth wealth, which hides money, from quiet luxury, which signals it discreetly, and from old money, which is narrower and concerns families that held wealth for at least two generations [1]. Their status is secure, so they have less need to signal it [1]. In the US, old money often describes a de facto aristocracy, whereas in the UK it refers more narrowly to nobility and landed gentry, and someone with old money there may be poor or insolvent [5].

The style traces to the late 18th and early 19th centuries, when the capitalist classes of Europe and America set themselves apart from courtly display through sober clothes and interiors, and to the Great Male Renunciation that moved men toward dark suits and muted colors [1]. In The Great Gatsby (1925), old-money characters see Gatsby's ostentation as vulgar new money [1].

Sociologists described the same distinction. W. Lloyd Warner's scheme, set out in Social Class in America (1960) from 1930s research, divided the upper class into upper-upper families, viewed as quasi-aristocratic, and lower-upper wealthy people from business, and in the early 20th century the upper-upper class was considered more prestigious than the nouveau riche even when the latter had more money [5]. Wikipedia adds that nouveau riche families built Gilded Age mansions modeled on European palaces while old money was more conservative [5].

In the 1990s Donna Karan and Miuccia Prada popularized streamlined, practical clothing for affluent professionals, and Jil Sander and Giorgio Armani are listed as precursors of the minimalist look [1]. Highsnobiety links the style to normcore and sprezzatura, citing Steve Jobs's black Issey Miyake turtlenecks as an example, and calls quiet luxury nothing new while noting its recent prominence [2].

A Ypulse item from August 2021, citing Vox, described preppy style, also called the old money aesthetic, resurfacing on social media alongside dark academia and the WASP look, with young users reviving khakis, oxford shirts, tweed blazers and tennis skirts in contrast to Y2K and streetwear trends [10]. Some were teaching peers the history of prep style, while others opposed it; one TikToker quoted there called it the peak of white supremacist fashion, and similar debates followed the 2020 Tokyo Olympic uniforms, with some calling for a rebrand [10].

The National reported on 22 May 2022 that the #oldmoney and #oldmoneyaesthetic hashtags had passed a billion views and that Highclere Castle, the Downton Abbey setting, appeared often in videos [6]. Men's looks were modeled on Gossip Girl's Nate Archibald and Elite's Guzman Nunier, with Prince Harry also named as an inspiration, while spin-off trends included old money names, houses and lifestyle [6]. The article called the trend class-conscious and exclusionary, quoting one user who said old money is not always pure class [6].

Wikipedia reports that social media and television carried the look to a wide audience in 2023, citing a March 2023 Vogue piece and a July 2023 New York Times article [1]. The HBO series Succession, which showed wealthy New Yorkers in expensive but understated clothing, fuelled the term Succession core, and Gwyneth Paltrow's March 2023 civil trial in Utah added attention because her wardrobe fit the style [1].

In a W Magazine interview dated 8 May 2023, the show's costume designer Michelle Matland said she did not think stealth wealth existed as a term before the show, and described old money as not interested in a logo world [11]. She tied Tom's wardrobe to his arc from boxy off-the-rack suits to high-end ones as he sought to belong to the one percent, and said a go-to uniform helps people under that kind of money and stress keep clothes from becoming part of their problem [11]. Kendall Roy's cashmere Loro Piana cap became the best-known single item; Matland said the production searched the country for it [11].

Economic context also features in accounts of the trend: after the pandemic people spent more on services and less on trendy goods, and recession fears led some to label the look recessioncore [1]. Highsnobiety floated social media, logo fatigue, economic anxiety and Succession as drivers and pointed to growth at Ermenegildo Zegna and rising market values at Hermes and other luxury houses [2]. By January 2024 the trend was seen as outdated, after Paris Fashion Week 2024 featured flashier styles [1].

subs.h: The revival and the timeless argument
paras: A December 2024 article in The Eagle said the aesthetic had grown since 2023, helped by the film Saltburn and the Gossip Girl revival, and argued it is timeless rather than a passing trend because of its emphasis on simplicity and fewer, better pieces [7].

Labels linked to quiet luxury include Loro Piana, Brunello Cucinelli, Zegna, Hermes, Brioni, Canali, Bottega Veneta and The Row; Jil Sander and Giorgio Armani are cited as minimalist precursors. Old-money heritage names include Savile Row houses such as Anderson & Sheppard and Huntsman, John Lobb and Turnbull & Asser [1]. Highsnobiety lists more accessible reference points for related sub-styles such as American prep, including Ralph Lauren, Lemaire, Aime Leon Dore and Allen Edmonds [2]. Shared traits are material and construction quality, timeless design, absent logos and premium pricing [1]. Brunello Cucinelli is associated with muted beige, white and sage palettes [1].

Advocates present the look as a low-risk way to appear well put together: Wikipedia notes that quiet luxury pieces are meant to last, which supports sustainability and long-term brand loyalty, though this can mean fewer purchases [1]. Highsnobiety describes the style as less about wealth than about confidence [2].

Research summarised on Wikipedia suggests people with less need to signal status prefer discreet or unbranded luxury, while those with stronger status anxiety choose visible logos [1]. Eckhardt and colleagues (2015) identified the spread of masstige luxury, affiliation with elite groups and appreciation of craftsmanship as drivers [1].

In looksmaxxing terms, the clothing is treated as a frame for the face and body: forum members pair it with low body fat and a neat haircut, and one member describes the style as something every normie likes because it is timeless [3][4].

Looksmax.org has threads titled around whether old money maxxing is legitimate, an old-money phenotype said to be voted highest appeal in 2022, and how to adopt the look [8][9]. In a thread by a member who is not from a wealthy background, who describes himself as 5'9" with about 16% body fat, he asks how to look old money without seeming like a poser; one reply suggests low body fat, a short trendy haircut and Massimo Dutti clothes at about 200 euros for an outfit with shoes [3].

Another member, who describes a lean, muscular body and already dresses in Ralph Lauren, loafers and loose jeans, asks whether archive fashion would make him less attractive than old money style, and a reply says old money is dated and another style has more appeal [4]. The Hacker News submission What Old Money Looks Like in America, and Who Pays for It had little discussion [12].

Commentators note that the look still functions as status signaling in a discreet form, and the label recessioncore suggests it partly reflected economic anxiety [1]. Coverage of the TikTok wave raised concerns that the aesthetic is class-conscious and tied to whiteness and privilege, while enthusiasts say it is about quality, history and fewer purchases [6][10][7]. Satirical takes exist, with Highsnobiety mentioning the Gstaad Guy account [2].

No studies found testing whether quiet luxury or old money dress improves attractiveness. Consumer research on status signaling, including the Eckhardt et al. (2015) work on understated luxury, is summarized above [1].

lore.intro: Members discuss old money dress as a safe, widely liked choice and argue over whether it works without the matching background or whether other styles have more appeal [3][4].
